desc:
A skyline is the region formed by n unit-wide columns standing side by side: column i covers the x-range [i, i+1] and the y-range [0, heights[i]]. You want to build exactly this region out of axis-aligned rectangles with integer corners. The rectangles must not overlap and must cover the region completely and nothing outside it.

Return the minimum number of rectangles needed. A column of height 0 is empty and is not part of the region.

Examples: [2, 3, 2, 3] needs 3 (one 3-wide 2-tall block, plus two single-column pieces on top). [3, 1, 3] needs 3 (a wide base and two towers), and [4, 4, 4] needs just 1.
hints: Start with small cases: a staircase going up, a valley ([3,1,3]) and a plateau. When does a new rectangle really have to start, and when can an existing one just be extended to the right?
Think of the rectangles that are still open as layers piled on top of each other, with strictly increasing top levels. A column of height h forces every open layer with a top above h to end.
Keep a stack of open top levels. For each column pop all levels greater than h. If the new top equals h, that layer simply continues; otherwise (and if h > 0) push h and count one new rectangle.
editorial: Scan the columns from left to right and maintain a stack of strictly increasing heights; each entry stands for a rectangle that is still being extended to the right, stacked above the entry below it (it spans from the level of the entry below up to its own level). When the next column has height h, every open rectangle that reaches higher than h has to be closed here, so pop all entries greater than h.

Now look at the new top. If it equals h, the rectangle ending at level h continues over this column for free. If it is lower (or the stack is empty) and h > 0, a new rectangle between that level and h must start at this column, so push h and add one to the answer. Equal neighbours and the plateau case therefore cost nothing, while valleys cost a new piece on the way back up. The answer is the number of pushes. Each column is pushed and popped at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space. A brute-force check over all tilings of small skylines confirms that this greedy count is minimal.
